title: Longer out than in
hook: slow breathing with a longer exhale tends to calm the body, a finding repeated in many lab studies

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was just watching: letting the breath breathe itself. Your line was it breathes. Today, you steer it, a little.

A near miss on the highway. A message that makes your face go hot. In moments like that, the breath often goes short and high, up in the chest, quick in and quick out. Then the danger passes, and a lot of people do something nobody taught them. They let out a long breath. Whew. Nobody gives lessons in whew. It's as if the body already knows something about the out-breath. Today, slow it down on purpose: longer out than in.

Your heart doesn't beat at one steady speed. When you breathe in, it tends to speed up a little. When you breathe out, it tends to slow down a little. You can feel this with two fingers on your wrist while you breathe slowly. The slowing on the out-breath is linked to the vagus nerve, a long nerve that runs from the brain down through the chest and belly, part of the body's rest-and-digest system. Make the out-breath longer than the in-breath, and you spend more of each minute in the slowing half. And it isn't only an idea. Researchers have slowed people's breathing in labs to around six breaths a minute, often with a longer exhale, and measured heart rate, blood pressure, and how calm people say they feel. Many of these studies find a calming effect. Most are small, and they don't all agree on the details, so the honest word is tends. A longer exhale tends to calm the body. It isn't a cure, and it won't fix what upset you. But it can turn the volume down enough for you to think. Older traditions paid attention to the out-breath too. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a yoga manual, gives the exhale its own name and its own place in breath practice, and singers, swimmers and flute players learn to make an out-breath last. The lab tests what the whew already knew.
screen: `IN SPEEDS UP, OUT SLOWS DOWN.` · `THE VAGUS NERVE.` · `SIX BREATHS A MINUTE, IN THE LAB.` · `IT TENDS TO CALM.` · then, large: `LONGER OUT.`

segments.voice: Sit with your back easy and your shoulders dropped, and breathe in through your nose for four, then out through your nose or softly through your lips for six. If six feels like too much, try five and let it grow; if you feel light-headed, go back to normal breathing for a while. No need to force it, just keep the out a little longer than the in.
Vagus. The nerve linked to the slowing on your out-breath; a longer exhale tends to calm it. Today's word.
Your line: longer out. The body already knew it; now you know it too. Day ninety-eight, done.
